title: Moto Guzzi 1200 8V roller-tappet kits are released only against a documented wear claim, not as prevention
description: Drawn from two Piaggio Group technical bulletins, text-extracted and read. The roller-tappet conversion for the 8V engines exists as three manufacturer kits selected by engine, with pads, a ground plate torqued to a stated figure, a shim, seals and gaskets all itemised. The bulletins are explicit that there are **no preventive operations**: the kit is released against a documented wear claim, with a dealer-tool reset afterwards, and out-of-warranty parts were made free through a help-desk ticket route. So a customer asking for the conversion 'before it fails' is asking for something the manufacturer's own process does not provide, and a shop should know that before promising it. Kit availability is currently unresolved — the fiche says 'contact' and one retailer shows a four-figure kit sold out.
symptoms: Customer requests preventive tappet conversion
Kit quoted as a stock item
Out-of-warranty engine with flat-tappet wear
causes: The manufacturer's bulletins release the kit against documented wear only, with no preventive fitment
Kit selection is by engine and the bulletin carries the table
Out-of-warranty supply ran through a help-desk ticket rather than a normal parts order
Current availability is unresolved and cannot be assumed
fix_procedure: Document the wear first — metal in the oil, the tappet faces — because that is what the manufacturer's process requires before a kit is released. Select the kit from the bulletin table by engine rather than by model, and use the bulletin's torque figure for the ground plate and its shim, seal and gasket numbers. Route an out-of-warranty claim through the manufacturer's help desk rather than assuming a retail order will succeed. Tell the customer plainly that preventive fitment is not what the manufacturer offers, and confirm kit availability before quoting a date.
parts_needed: Roller tappet kit selected by engine from the bulletin table
Pads, ground plate, shim, seals and gaskets as itemised in the bulletin

title: No MV Agusta 'rim band' part could be established — the documented spoked-wheel fix is a whole rear wheel
description: Drawn from the manufacturer's dealer communication and trade coverage of a 2017 campaign, checked against the fiche. Phase 233 recorded that the Dragster's loose-spoke campaign was remedied by replacing the rear wheel because the nipples' surface treatment could not hold torque. This phase looked for the part a shop would expect to stock for a tubeless spoked MV — a rim seal band — and could not establish one on the fiche. The documented remedy for the spoked-wheel defect is a **complete rear wheel**, fitted by the dealer, on a small production run over a stated window. So there is no consumable to order here; a spoked-wheel complaint on these machines is a frame-number question and then a wheel, not a band. The campaign is described without a reference number, per this project's standing decision.
model: Dragster RR with spoked wheels, 2017 campaign population
symptoms: Loose or loosening rear spokes
Customer asks for a rim band or seal
Spoked-wheel complaint on a Dragster
causes: No rim seal band part number could be established on the MV fiche
The documented defect is spoke-nipple surface treatment, and the remedy is a new rear wheel
A campaign covered a small population over a stated window, by frame number
A shop expecting a KTM-style consumable will look for a part that does not exist
fix_procedure: Check the frame number against the campaign first, and do not re-tension the spokes — Phase 233 records why the torque cannot hold. Where the machine is in the campaign, the remedy is a dealer-fitted rear wheel. Where it is not, treat the wheel as the unit of repair rather than searching for a band that this phase could not find. Do not quote a rim band for an MV until a part number is confirmed on the fiche.
parts_needed: Complete rear wheel where the campaign applies

title: The Aprilia V4 charging system exists in two families, and the fiche has folded one of them into a single number
description: Drawn from Aprilia's parts fiche, read this phase. The RSV4 and Tuono V4 carry two distinct flywheel-and-stator families: an early Mitsubishi-type assembly under one number, and a Kokusan-type family whose two earlier numbers have both been superseded into one current number. The fiche assigns the early type to the first RSV4 years and the Tuono V4 R of the first year, and the Kokusan type from the APRC generation onward. Aftermarket sellers quote an engine-number threshold for the split; **no Aprilia document states that threshold**, and the fiche assigns by model year and variant instead. So the fitted type is established from the machine, not from a number a seller quotes, and the reduced-magnet flywheel that Phase 237 names as the first suspect on a burnt stator exists for the Kokusan family only.
symptoms: Stator ordered by year fits the wrong type
Seller quotes an engine-number cut-off
Two RSV4s of one year take different parts
causes: Two charging families exist on the same model, assigned by the fiche by year and variant
Two earlier Kokusan-type numbers have been superseded into one current number
The engine-number split in circulation is an aftermarket claim with no Aprilia document behind it
A burnt stator on the early family has a different remedy set from the later one
fix_procedure: Identify the charging family from the machine before ordering — open the generator cover if necessary — rather than from the model year alone or from a seller's engine-number threshold. Order the current superseded number for the Kokusan family; the fiche chain is recorded in the catalogue. On the early Mitsubishi family, the aftermarket kit that replaces the original number exists but the reduced-magnet flywheel does not, so the Phase 237 flywheel-first differential applies to the later family only.
parts_needed: Flywheel-and-stator assembly to the current fiche number for the fitted family

title: 'BMW supplies the hexhead final drive only as a complete unit' is not established — bearings and seals carry their own numbers
description: Drawn from a parts retailer's catalogue and owner reports, checked against a claim made elsewhere. A widely repeated statement, and one an earlier research pass in this project produced, is that BMW will not supply hexhead final-drive internals and sells only the complete drive. This phase looked for the document and did not find it; what it found instead is that the crown-wheel bearing and the wheel-side bearing **carry individual BMW part numbers**, are stocked by independent retailers at two-figure prices, and have dimension-matched industrial equivalents. One owner's dealer account of being refused internals in a particular year is an owner report about one dealer, not a policy. The distinction decides a quote: a bearing at under a hundred dollars against a complete final drive at four figures.
model: R1200 hexhead and camhead final drives
symptoms: Final drive quoted as a complete unit only
Told BMW will not supply the bearing
Owner cites a dealer refusal as policy
causes: The 'complete unit only' claim circulates without a BMW document behind it
Individual bearing and seal numbers exist and are retailed independently
A single dealer's refusal in one year is reported as manufacturer policy
The two quotes differ by more than an order of magnitude
fix_procedure: Quote the bearing and seal by their individual part numbers before quoting a complete final drive, and source from an independent retailer if a dealer declines. Establish which bearing is failing — the outer wheel-side ball bearing is the one owners identify, and it is a standard dimensional envelope — and confirm the number on the fiche by production month, because the design changed around 2010. Forum tip: owners report that the wheel-side bearing's dimensions match a common industrial deep-groove bearing, which is a fallback when the BMW number is on back-order; treat that as approximate and confirm the seal arrangement.
parts_needed: Final drive bearing by individual BMW number

title: The Ducati Desmoquattro opening rocker arm is discontinued, and the replacement is re-plating or tool steel
description: Drawn from Ducati's parts fiche and specialist vendors. The opening rocker arm for the 16-valve Desmoquattro — the part whose hard chrome flakes into the oil, per Phase 237 — is marked discontinued on the fiche for the models it was assigned to. What remains is a choice between two routes with different economics: a specialist exchange re-chroming service at a modest per-arm price, or aftermarket tool-steel rockers at a four-figure price per set. Neither is a Ducati part. A shop that quotes 'replace the rocker' against the fiche will find nothing to order, and needs to have chosen a route and told the customer before the covers come off.
model: Desmoquattro — Monster S4R 2003–06, ST4 S 2003–05 on the fiche; 916–998 family by aftermarket fitment
symptoms: Rocker arm shows discontinued on the fiche
Chrome flakes found in the oil
Rocker quote returns no orderable part
causes: The OEM opening rocker is discontinued for its fiche-assigned models
Re-chroming is an exchange service, so the customer's own rockers go away and come back
Tool-steel aftermarket rockers are a different material at a much higher price
Aftermarket fitment claims span engine families the fiche does not, and are the maker's claims
fix_procedure: Decide the route before disassembly: exchange re-plating keeps the cost down but means a turnaround with the engine open, while tool-steel rockers are immediate but expensive. Confirm fitment for the specific engine with the vendor, since the aftermarket claims cover families the fiche does not assign the OEM number to. Set clearances accurately on reassembly, which is reported to reduce recurrence of the flaking on plated rockers.
parts_needed: Re-chromed exchange rockers or tool-steel aftermarket rockers

title: Triumph's fiche does not itemise the Street Triple idle-valve hoses that fail — the orderable unit is different
description: Drawn from Triumph's parts fiche. Phase 237 records that warm high idle on the Sagem-era triples is usually the rubber hoses from the idle air control valve to the intake ports perishing, not the valve. This phase went to order those hoses and found that the fiche does not itemise them as such: the idle valve itself is listed with a VIN split between two numbers, and a set of hose numbers exists, but the specific IACV-to-port rubber hoses named by owners are not a separately orderable line. The orderable unit differs from the failing component, and a shop that orders the hose numbers on the fiche expecting the IACV hoses may receive something else.
model: Street Triple 675 2007–2016; the same layout on other Sagem-era triples
symptoms: Hose ordered from the fiche is not the failed one
IACV hoses not found as a line item
Two IACV numbers for one model
causes: The fiche itemises the idle valve and a set of hoses, but not the IACV-to-port rubber hoses as a separate part
The idle valve number splits by VIN, so the wrong one is easy to order
The failing component and the orderable unit are not the same thing
Owners source the rubber hoses generically by bore and length
fix_procedure: Identify the failed hose on the machine and measure it before ordering anything, because the fiche will not name it directly. Check the VIN against the split before ordering the idle valve, if the valve is genuinely at fault. Where the rubber hoses are the failure, expect to source them generically by bore and length or as part of a larger assembly, and confirm on the throttle-body diagram what each fiche hose number actually is.
parts_needed: Rubber hose by measured bore and length, or the fiche assembly that contains it
Idle air control valve to the correct VIN split, only if the valve tests faulty

title: KTM Adventure tubeless rim seal bands and bead gaskets are KTM-only parts, split by wheel size and by R or non-R
description: Drawn from KTM's parts fiche, read this phase. The rim seal band that Phase 225B records KTM ageing out at five years regardless of wear is not a generic consumable — no aftermarket equivalent was found — and it is not one part. The fiche splits it by front wheel size, which follows whether the machine is an R variant or not, and the rear band and its bead gasket are separate numbers again. A research pass in this project proposed a model pattern for the 19-inch band that would have matched the R variants, which take the 21-inch band; the catalogue rows here use exact model names for that reason. Ordering by 'Adventure' gets the wrong band about half the time.
model: 1190 Adventure and Adventure R, 1290 Super Adventure and R, 1090 Adventure R
symptoms: Band ordered for an Adventure does not fit
No aftermarket band found
Slow leak after a tyre change on a spoked KTM
causes: The band is KTM-only with no aftermarket equivalent found
Front band size follows the R or non-R wheel, so the model name without its suffix is ambiguous
Rear band and bead gasket are separate numbers
A five-year replacement recommendation means the part is ordered more often than a failure-only part would be
fix_procedure: Order by the exact model name including the R suffix and the wheel size, never by 'Adventure', and take the number from the machine's own wheel diagram on the fiche. Order the bead gasket with the rear band. Stock is KTM-only, so allow dealer lead time when a tyre change on a five-year-old machine is booked — the band should be replaced at that visit per KTM's recommendation, and finding it unavailable on the day means refitting a tyre onto an aged band.
parts_needed: Front rim seal band to the wheel size fitted

title: The KTM LC8 fiche pages for the balancer seal and starter freewheel are truncated, so 'not listed' does not mean 'does not fit'
description: Drawn from KTM's parts fiche, read this phase, with a correction from refutation. The balancer shaft seal that Phase 237 names for an oily front intake, and the starter freewheel whose bolts back out into the stator, both show fiche assignments to the 950 Super Enduro R and the 990 Super Duke, with a 990 Adventure diagram also carrying the freewheel. A research pass concluded from that page that the parts are 'scoped to 950/990 only' and that no 1190 or 1290 is listed. A refuter found the page **states that some compatible models are not shown** — the assignment list is truncated. So the absence of the later twins from that page is not evidence about them, and the honest state is unknown until their own model diagrams are read.
model: 950 and 990 LC8 on the fiche; 1190/1290 fitment unknown, not excluded
symptoms: Fiche page lists fewer models than expected
Part assumed not to fit a later twin
Assignment page shows a truncation note
causes: The fiche's assignment page for these numbers is explicitly truncated
A truncated list was read as a complete one
Absence from a truncated page was reported as exclusion
The later twins' own diagrams were not read
fix_procedure: Read the part from the specific machine's own diagram rather than from the part number's assignment page when that page carries a truncation note. Treat 'not listed' on a truncated page as unknown rather than as no-fit, and say so to the customer if asked. For the 950 and 990 the assignments are read and recorded; for the 1190 and 1290, check their model diagrams directly before ordering or ruling out.

title: Aprilia and Moto Guzzi share one parts catalogue, one supersession chain and one help-desk route
description: Drawn from the Piaggio Group's parts fiche and its technical bulletins, read this phase. Phase 236 records that these two makes share a dealer tool. They also share a parts system: the same group catalogue serves both, supersessions are carried the same way, and the manufacturer's bulletin route for an out-of-warranty parts claim — a help-desk ticket, used for the Guzzi tappet kits — is a group process rather than a Guzzi one. For a workshop that is quoting both makes, that means one supersession lookup habit, one bulletin archive to search, and one escalation route, rather than two of each. It also means a superseded number on one make's fiche can resolve to a part that the other make's models share.
model: All Piaggio Group motorcycle marques — Aprilia and Moto Guzzi
symptoms: Two makes researched as two parts systems
Supersession missed on one make and found on the other
Out-of-warranty claim routed to the wrong channel
causes: Both marques sit on one group parts catalogue
Supersession chains are recorded the same way for both
The bulletin and help-desk route is a group process
Marque-by-marque research hides the shared system
fix_procedure: Search supersessions and technical bulletins at group level rather than per marque, and use the group help-desk route for an out-of-warranty parts claim on either make. When a part number appears discontinued on one marque's fiche, check the group catalogue for the superseding number before concluding it is unavailable. Treat the two makes as one parts relationship when deciding whether to take on the work.

title: The BMW ELAST belt designation 'disagreement' has an explanation: BMW prints production length, Continental prints fitted length
description: Drawn from Continental's designation table as reproduced by owners, checked against BMW dealer and retailer listings. A research pass in this project recorded that sources disagree on which Contitech designation matches which BMW alternator belt, and declined to pick one. A refuter found the explanation in the same owner thread: **BMW marks the belt with its production length and Continental with its fitted length**, so BMW's 4PK582 corresponds to Continental's 4PK592 (582) and BMW's 4PK592 to Continental's 4PK611 (592). The two belts are different generations of the ELAST stretch-fit — one for the early hexhead, one for the later — and the research had paired them the wrong way round. The catalogue rows here carry the corrected pairing at an approximate rating, because the source is an owner-reproduced table rather than a Continental document.
model: R1200 hexhead 2004–2007 (4PK592) and 2005–2014 with R nineT (4PK582)
symptoms: Belt designations look mismatched between vendors
Two ELAST belts for overlapping years
Aftermarket belt ordered by number does not fit
causes: BMW and Continental print different lengths for the same belt — production versus fitted
Two ELAST generations exist with overlapping model-year fitment
The overlap for 2005–07 means model year alone does not choose the belt
The pairing in circulation was reversed
fix_procedure: Choose the belt by the BMW part number from the fiche by production month, not by the designation printed on the belt and not by model year alone, because the two generations overlap for 2005 to 2007. When cross-referencing to an aftermarket belt, use the corrected pairing recorded in the catalogue and treat it as approximate. Forum tip: owners note the printed designation on the fitted belt, before removal, and match the replacement to that rather than to a listing.
parts_needed: ELAST alternator belt to the BMW number for the production month

title: The Moto Guzzi small-block oil filter has no Hiflo cross-reference, while the big-block one does
description: Drawn from Hiflofiltro's own catalogue and the Moto Guzzi fiche. The current small-block filter — the V7, V9 and V85 number, which supersedes an earlier one — is a low-cost part with a manufacturer number that independent retailers stock. Hiflo's own catalogue carries **no cross-reference** for it, while the big-block Griso and Stelvio filter cross-references cleanly. For a shop used to reaching for the Hiflo book, this is the one where it comes up empty, and the honest answer is that the manufacturer part is the part. The catalogue records the supersession from the earlier small-block number so that an older fiche reference still resolves.
model: V7, V9, V85 small block (no Hiflo); Griso, Stelvio big block (Hiflo cross-references)
symptoms: Hiflo lookup returns nothing for a small-block Guzzi
Filter ordered by an old superseded number
Big-block cross-reference applied to a small block
causes: Hiflo's catalogue has no entry for the current small-block filter number
The big-block filter does cross-reference, which invites the assumption that the small block does too
The small-block number supersedes an earlier one that older references still cite
The manufacturer part is inexpensive and stocked, so there is little aftermarket pressure
fix_procedure: Order the manufacturer filter for the small-block engines by its current number, and do not assume a Hiflo equivalent exists because one does for the big block. Resolve an older reference through the supersession recorded in the catalogue. For the big-block engines the Hiflo cross-reference is exact and can be used.
parts_needed: Moto Guzzi small-block oil filter by current number
